content: The following studies provide insights into various mental health interventions aimed at promoting well-being and preventing mental health issues among adolescents: 1. Arnason and Craighead (2009) explored strategies to prevent depression in Icelandic adolescents, with a follow-up study in 2011 demonstrating the long-term effectiveness of these interventions over 12 months. 2. Asarnow et al. (2009) examined the long-term benefits of short-term quality improvement interventions for depressed youth in primary care settings, highlighting sustained improvements in mental health outcomes. 3. Balle and Tortella-Feliu (2010) evaluated a brief school-based program targeting childhood anxiety, demonstrating its efficacy in selective prevention. 4. Bella-Awusah et al. (2016) assessed the effectiveness of group cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for depressed adolescents in southwest Nigeria, showing significant improvements in mental health. 5. Berry and Hunt (2009) evaluated an intervention program for anxious adolescent boys who experienced bullying, finding it effective in reducing anxiety symptoms. 6. Boniel-Nissim and Barak (2013) investigated the therapeutic value of blogging for adolescents dealing with social-emotional difficulties, showing positive outcomes in emotional expression and coping. 7. Cui et al. (2016) implemented a brief group CBT program to prevent depressive symptoms in Chinese college students, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing symptoms. 8. De Cuyper et al. (2004) conducted a pilot study on treating depressive symptoms in schoolchildren, showing promising results in symptom reduction. 9. Dingle and Fay (2017) evaluated a group emotion regulation program using music listening for young adults, finding it effective in improving emotional regulation. 10. Dobson et al. (2010) conducted a randomized controlled trial to prevent depression and anxiety in high-risk adolescents, demonstrating the program's efficacy. 11. Fukumori et al. (2017) examined the impact of a guided, structured writing program on self-harm ideation and emotion regulation, showing significant benefits. 12. Fung et al. (2016, 2019) evaluated school-based mindfulness interventions for ethnic minority youth, identifying mediators and moderators of intervention effects. 13. Gaesser and Karan (2017) compared the emotional freedom technique with CBT for reducing adolescent anxiety, finding both approaches effective. 14. Gaete et al. (2016) conducted a randomized controlled trial of a school-based intervention to improve depressive symptoms in at-risk Chilean adolescents, showing positive outcomes. 15. Gau et al. (2012) explored how negative life events and substance use moderated the effects of a CBT-based depression prevention program for adolescents. 16. Gawrysiak et al. (2009) tested behavioral activation for moderately depressed university students, demonstrating its effectiveness in symptom reduction. 17. Geisner et al. (2006) evaluated a brief mailed intervention for depressive symptoms, finding it effective in reducing symptoms. 18. Gillham et al. (2006) studied the Penn Resiliency Program in primary care settings, showing its success in preventing depression among early adolescents. 19. Hetrick et al. (2017) assessed internet-based CBT for young people with suicide-related behavior, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing symptoms. 20. Hill and Pettit (2016) piloted the LEAP intervention to reduce adolescents' perceived burdensomeness, showing promising results. 21. Hoek et al. (2012) evaluated internet-based guided self-help problem-solving therapy for adolescents with depression and anxiety, finding it effective. 22. Hunt et al. (2009) conducted a randomized controlled trial of an early intervention program for adolescent anxiety disorders, showing significant improvements. 23. Ip et al. (2016) tested a culturally attuned internet-based depression prevention program for Chinese adolescents, demonstrating its effectiveness. 24. Jacob et al. (2016) evaluated a bibliotherapy-based intervention for depressed Filipino female adolescents, showing positive outcomes. 25. Jolly et al. (2018) piloted a cognitive-behavioral intervention for children with unusual experiences and emotional symptoms, finding it acceptable and clinically useful. 26. Khanna and Singh (2016) studied the impact of gratitude education on well-being indicators among North Indian adolescents, showing significant improvements. 27. King et al. (2015) developed the Teen Options for Change intervention for young emergency patients at risk of suicide, demonstrating its effectiveness. 28. Kramer et al. (2014) tested a web-based solution-focused brief chat treatment for depressed adolescents, finding it effective in symptom reduction. 29. Kwok et al. (2016) evaluated a positive psychology intervention to alleviate child depression and increase life satisfaction, showing significant benefits. 30. Livheim et al. (2015) assessed the effectiveness of acceptance and commitment therapy for adolescent mental health, reporting positive outcomes. 31. Martinsen et al. (2019) evaluated the EMOTION program for preventing anxiety and depression in schoolchildren, demonstrating its effectiveness. 32. McArthur et al. (2013) piloted school-based humanistic counseling for psychological distress in young people, showing promising results. 33. McCarty et al. (2011) tested the feasibility of the Positive Thoughts and Actions prevention program for middle schoolers at risk for depression, finding it effective. 34. Merry et al. (2012) evaluated SPARX, a computerized self-help intervention for adolescent depression, demonstrating its non-inferiority to traditional treatments. 35. Miller et al. (2011) conducted two randomized trials of a preventive intervention for child anxiety, showing significant reductions in symptoms. 36. Nieto and Barraca (2017) compared behavioral activation and cognitive restructuring for reducing automatic negative thoughts in anxiety-provoking situations, finding both effective. 37. Noel et al. (2013) studied depression prevention among rural preadolescent girls, showing positive outcomes. 38. Pearce et al. (2017) evaluated school-based humanistic counseling for psychological distress in an ethnically diverse sample, demonstrating its effectiveness. 39. Peden et al. (2001) reported on an 18-month follow-up of a depression prevention program for high-risk college women, showing sustained benefits. 40. Poppelaars et al. (2016) compared two CBT programs for adolescent girls with subclinical depression, finding both effective. 41. Puskar et al. (2003) evaluated the Teaching Kids to Cope program for rural adolescents, showing improvements in depression and coping outcomes. 42. Pybis et al. (2015) piloted school-based humanistic counseling for psychological distress, reporting positive outcomes and methodological insights. 43. Reid et al. (2011) tested a mobile phone application for youth mental health assessment and management, finding it effective. 44. Roberts et al. (2003, 2004) studied the prevention of depressive symptoms in rural schoolchildren, showing positive outcomes in initial and follow-up studies. 45. Rohde et al. (2014, 2015) evaluated CBT-based group depression prevention programs, finding them effective in reducing symptoms over time. 46. Saelid and Nordahl (2017) tested rational emotive behavior therapy in high schools, showing its effectiveness in educating youth about mental health. 47. Sang and Tan (2018) evaluated a social skills training program for reducing internalizing behavior disorder symptoms in Chinese students, demonstrating its effectiveness. 48. Scholten et al. (2016) tested the effectiveness of a 3D video game for anxiety prevention among adolescents, showing promising results. 49. Sheffield et al. (2006) evaluated universal, indicated, and combined CBT approaches for preventing depression among adolescents, finding all approaches effective. 50. Smith et al. (2015) tested computerized CBT for depressed adolescents, showing significant symptom reduction. 51. Spence et al. (2003) evaluated the Problem-Solving for Life program for preventing adolescent depression, demonstrating its effectiveness. 52. Stallard et al. (2013) conducted a cluster randomized trial of classroom-based CBT for high-risk adolescents, showing clinical and cost-effectiveness. 53. Stasiak et al. (2014) piloted a computer-based CBT program for adolescents with depressive symptoms, showing positive outcomes. 54. Stice et al. (2007, 2010) evaluated brief depression prevention programs for high-risk adolescents, demonstrating their efficacy over time. 55. Takagaki et al. (2016, 2018) tested behavioral activation programs for late adolescents with subthreshold depression, showing enduring effects. 56. Topper et al. (2017) targeted excessive worry and rumination in adolescents to prevent anxiety and depression, demonstrating the program's effectiveness. 57. Wijnhoven et al. (2014) tested a depression prevention program for adolescent girls with elevated depressive symptoms, showing significant benefits. 58. Woods and Jose (2011) evaluated a school-based early intervention program for Maori and Pacific adolescents, demonstrating its effectiveness. 59. Wright et al. (2017) tested computerized CBT for depression in adolescents, reporting feasibility and positive outcomes. 60. Young et al. (2006, 2009, 2010, 2012, 2016, 2018) conducted multiple trials of interpersonal psychotherapy-adolescent skills training, showing its efficacy in preventing depression and addressing comorbid anxiety. 61. Zandkarimi et al. (2018) tested nonviolent communication interventions to reduce stress, anxiety, and depression in young Iranian women, showing significant improvements. These studies collectively highlight the diverse and effective approaches to promoting mental health and preventing mental health issues among adolescents, including CBT, mindfulness, behavioral activation, and interpersonal psychotherapy.
